title: Adalaj Ni Vav (Adalaj Stepwell)
summary: Gujarat Tourism describes Adalaj Ni Vav as a 15th-century stepwell with five storeys, Indo-Islamic fusion architecture, and ornamental carvings; its exact construction year is not specified in that listing.
unverified: Exact construction year is not specified by the cited Gujarat Tourism listing; other online accounts give differing years.
Builder, patronage and popular historical narratives are not established by the cited source.
The source does not establish the material composition of the complete structure; materials are left blank.
Coordinates are approximate map-placement coordinates, not survey data.
source_title: Adalaj Ni Vav Gandhinagar — Gujarat Tourism
verified_facts: Gujarat Tourism describes the site as a 15th-century stepwell in Gandhinagar.
Its listing identifies five storeys, three entrances, and an octagonal well opening.
The listing describes Indo-Islamic fusion architecture and ornamental carvings.
Ami khumbor and Kalp vriksha carvings are described as carved from a single slab of stone.

title: Rani-ki-Vav (the Queen's Stepwell)
summary: UNESCO describes Rani-ki-Vav at Patan as an 11th-century stepwell, initially built as a memorial to a king and designed as an inverted temple, with seven stair levels and sculptural panels.
unverified: The exact construction year and identity of the commemorated king are not established by the cited UNESCO description.
Construction materials are not specified in the cited source; materials are left blank.
Coordinates are approximate map-placement values converted from a Government of India listing; their datum and survey precision are not stated.
source_title: Rani-ki-Vav (the Queen’s Stepwell) at Patan, Gujarat — UNESCO World Heritage Centre
verified_facts: UNESCO locates the stepwell at Patan on the banks of the Saraswati River and dates it to the 11th century.
UNESCO says it was initially built as a memorial to a king and designed as an inverted temple.
The site description identifies seven levels of stairs, sculptural panels, a rectangular tank, and a well shaft.

title: Sun Temple, Modhera
summary: The UNESCO Tentative List describes Modhera's east-facing Sun Temple as an 11th-century Maru-Gurjara sandstone complex with a main shrine, assembly hall, sacred pool and extensive sculpture; map coordinates are approximate.
unverified: The exact construction year is not established by the selected UNESCO source; its century attribution is stylistic.
The WGS84 coordinate is approximate map placement and is not a surveyed coordinate verified by UNESCO.
No materials beyond the stated bright yellow sandstone are asserted.
source_title: Sun Temple, Modhera and its adjoining monuments — UNESCO Tentative List
verified_facts: The UNESCO Tentative List places the temple in Mehsana District, Gujarat, on the left bank of the Pushpavati River in Becharaji Taluka.
The entry describes an east-facing temple built of bright yellow sandstone in the Maru-Gurjara style.
The complex includes the main shrine, Gudhamandapa, Sabhamandapa or Rangamandapa, and a sacred Kunda.
UNESCO characterizes the complex as 11th-century architecture and presents the dating as an inference from style.

title: Sidi Saiyyed Mosque
features: continues to function as a place of prayer
summary: Gujarat Tourism dates the Sidi Saiyyed Mosque in Ahmedabad to 1572-73 CE and describes its tree-of-life jali windows and continuing use for prayer; the map coordinates are approximate.
unverified: The source places the mosque in Ahmedabad but does not state coordinates; the map pin is approximate.

source_title: Siddi Sayed Mosque Ahmedabad — Gujarat Tourism
verified_facts: Gujarat Tourism identifies the mosque in Ahmedabad and dates it to 1572–73 CE.
The listing describes jali windows with intertwining branches forming a tree-of-life motif.
It notes that the central arch lacks intricate latticework and that the mosque continues to be used for prayer.

title: Lothal
period: Harappan culture (c. 2400-1600 BCE per UNESCO Tentative List)
features: basin identified as a tidal dockyard
summary: UNESCO's Tentative List describes Lothal as a Harappan port-town with upper and lower town areas and a basin interpreted as a tidal dockyard; the coordinates are approximate map-placement coordinates.
unverified: The listed period is the broad Harappan culture range in the cited UNESCO record, not a precise construction date for the site.
The exact site boundaries are not represented by the approximate map pin.
Lothal is on UNESCO's Tentative List; this record does not imply World Heritage inscription.
source_title: Archaeological remains of a Harappa Port-Town, Lothal — UNESCO Tentative List
verified_facts: UNESCO locates the remains in Dholka Taluk, Ahmedabad district, Gujarat, along the Bhogava river.
The tentative-list record gives a Harappan culture evidence range of 2400 BCE to 1600 BCE.
UNESCO describes upper and lower town areas and a basin interpreted as a tidal dockyard.
The description notes mud-brick platforms in the upper town, streets, drains, and a bead-making area.
